prompt: On an ordinary switch, what does a device get the moment its cable is plugged in?

choices.text: Nothing until an administrator approves its address in the console
choices.why: That is what NAC adds; an ordinary port asks nothing.

choices.text: The whole segment, with no question asked
choices.why: Right. It can send to every machine there.

choices.text: Only the internet, never the internal machines
choices.why: A switch does not know internet from internal; the segment is open.

choices.text: Only DHCP, until its owner logs in to Windows
choices.why: Logging in to the device says nothing to the switch.

prompt: Why does a filter on port-desk in sw see every frame desk sends?

choices.text: Because sw copies all traffic of the segment to a monitoring port
choices.why: No mirror is involved; it is the port itself.

choices.text: The port is where desk's cable arrives, before the bridge
choices.why: Right. That is the position of a managed switch's port security.

choices.text: Because desk routes all its traffic through sw as a gateway
choices.why: desk has no gateway in the lab; sw switches, it does not route.

choices.text: Because every machine in the lab shares one network card
choices.why: Each has its own card and its own port.

prompt: Why is the MAC filter a netdev table hooked on ingress of port-desk?

choices.text: It sees frames as they arrive on that one interface
choices.why: Right. Before the bridge forwards them anywhere.

choices.text: Because only netdev tables are allowed to use counters
choices.why: Counters work in any table.

choices.text: Because the inet family cannot read IPv4 addresses
choices.why: It can; the point is seeing layer 2 at the port.

choices.text: Because hostapd refuses to start if any other table exists on the switch
choices.why: hostapd does not read nftables at all.

prompt: With the address ending in :99, the counter showed 2 dropped packets of 56 bytes, and no ICMP. Why no ICMP?
hint: What does a machine need before it can send a ping on a segment?

choices.text: The filter dropped the pings before counting them
choices.why: The counter sits on the drop path; anything dropped is counted.

choices.text: ping refuses to send from a card whose address was changed
choices.why: ping does not know or care.

choices.text: Its ARP requests got no answer, so the ping never left
choices.why: Right. 28 bytes each: two ARP requests.

choices.text: web answered from a different interface that the counter does not watch
choices.why: web never heard a request.

prompt: What does sticky MAC do on a managed switch?

choices.text: It assigns each new device a random address so nobody can be tracked
choices.why: That is MAC randomisation, a privacy feature of devices.

choices.text: It checks the device's certificate
choices.why: Certificates are 802.1X; sticky MAC only learns an address.

choices.text: Learns the first address on a port and refuses others
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: It sends the address to RADIUS as a username
choices.why: That is MAC authentication bypass.

prompt: Why did the printer's address let desk through the filter?

choices.text: The printer was switched off, so the switch reassigned its slot
choices.why: The list has no slots; it compares values.

choices.text: Because the filter was loaded before the printer's address was added
choices.why: The address was in the file from the start.

choices.text: The filter checks an address the sender writes
choices.why: Right. A claim, not an identity.

choices.text: Because desk and the printer share the reception's IP address
choices.why: The filter never looks at IP addresses.

prompt: When is MAC authentication bypass for a printer safe enough?

choices.text: When the address only reaches what a printer needs, such as the print server
choices.why: Right. A laptop pretending to be the printer then gains nothing.

choices.text: When the printer's address is kept secret
choices.why: It is on a label and in every frame it sends.

choices.text: When the RADIUS server checks the address twice
choices.why: Checking a claim twice does not make it proof.

choices.text: Never; MAB must be switched off on every port
choices.why: Then the printer cannot be on the network at all.

prompt: Which of these can a switch or a monitor notice about a copied printer address? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The same address on two ports at once
choices.why: Both devices are up.

choices.text: A port whose address changes
choices.why: Sticky MAC turns it into a shutdown.

choices.text: A printer opening SSH connections to the portal
choices.why: Behaviour unlike its kind.

choices.text: The colour of the cable plugged into the socket
choices.why: Nothing on the network sees a cable.

prompt: Match each 802.1X role with what plays it in the lab.
What does an unauthorised 802.1X port forward?

choices.text: Nothing at all, not even the login
choices.why: Then the device could never log in.

choices.text: Only EAPOL frames, so the device can still log in
choices.why: Right. Ethernet type 0x888e.

choices.text: DHCP and DNS, so the device can find the RADIUS server
choices.why: The device never talks to RADIUS; the switch does.

choices.text: Everything, but logged until the login completes
choices.why: Logging is not closing.

prompt: A laptop on PEAP is configured to accept any server certificate. What does that risk?

choices.text: That the laptop's own certificate expires early
choices.why: With PEAP the laptop has a password, not a certificate.

choices.text: Nothing: the server still checks the laptop's password
choices.why: Which server? It hands the password to whoever answers.

choices.text: Handing its password to whatever answers on the port
choices.why: Right. The supplicant must check the server.

choices.text: That the switch falls back to MAC authentication bypass
choices.why: The switch does not know how the laptop checks certificates.

prompt: Why does desk send a signing request to sw instead of receiving a key made there?

choices.text: Because openssl on sw cannot create elliptic-curve keys
choices.why: It created the CA's and the switch's.

choices.text: So the private key exists only on desk
choices.why: Right. A copied key also exists elsewhere.

choices.text: Because scp can copy requests but not keys
choices.why: scp copies any file.

choices.text: Because a key made on the switch would expire with the switch's certificate
choices.why: Keys do not expire with other certificates.

prompt: Right after hostapd and nac.nft are loaded, desk's ping to web fails. Why?

choices.text: hostapd crashed while starting on the wired driver
choices.why: It reported the port enabled.

choices.text: web refuses ICMP once 802.1X is configured anywhere
choices.why: web knows nothing of 802.1X.

choices.text: The old MAC filter is still loaded on the port
choices.why: It was deleted at the end of the MAC section.

choices.text: Nothing has logged in on the port yet, so only EAPOL passes
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Logged in with its own address, desk switches to the printer's address and loses the network. Why?

choices.text: The port opened for the address that logged in, not the new one
choices.why: Right. The set holds :14, and :63 is not in it.

choices.text: Changing the address logged the supplicant off
choices.why: It came back as soon as the address was restored, with no new login.

choices.text: The printer's certificate was revoked by the CA
choices.why: The printer has no certificate in this lab.

choices.text: hostapd detected two devices and closed the port
choices.why: The port reopened for :14 at once.

prompt: With dynamic VLAN assignment, what decides which network a wall socket gives?

choices.text: The socket's label, configured on the switch port
choices.why: That is the static way the feature replaces.

choices.text: The credential that logged in, as judged by RADIUS
choices.why: Right. RADIUS returns the VLAN with the acceptance.

choices.text: The device's operating system, read from its DHCP request
choices.why: DHCP comes after; the VLAN is set at login.

choices.text: Whichever VLAN has the most free addresses at that moment
choices.why: Placement follows identity, not capacity.

prompt: Why is a posture report weaker evidence than a certificate?

choices.text: Because posture agents only run on Windows
choices.why: Agents exist for several systems; the weakness is elsewhere.

choices.text: Because RADIUS cannot carry posture attributes
choices.why: Posture reaches the server; the issue is who wrote it.

choices.text: It is the device describing itself
choices.why: Right. An assertion again, harder to imitate than a MAC.

choices.text: Because posture is checked only once a year
choices.why: It is checked at login.

desk's ping to web goes through

items: sw creates the authority's key and certificate
desk creates its key and a signing request
the request is copied to sw
the authority signs it for clientAuth
desk fetches the certificate and the authority's

pairs.right: the device claims a listed address
the device holds a key the network signed

right_distractors: the device is free of malware
